subject: HINDU RELIGIOUS EDUCATION
title: Essence of Scriptures
overview: Scriptures are the sacred writings of a faith. This sub-strand draws lessons from the early books of the Ramayan, from the Jain texts Kalpasutra and Uttradhyana, from the Buddhist Dhammapada and Sigalovaada Sutta, and from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. You will learn the message of each and how to live it.

lessons.title: Why scriptures matter
objectives: Name the scriptures studied in this sub-strand and the faith each belongs to.
lessons.intro: A storybook can entertain you for an evening. A scripture is treated differently. People of faith read it, listen to it, bow before it or recite it because they believe it carries a message for how to live.
lessons.notes:
### What scripture means
A scripture is a sacred book or collection of teachings. It may contain stories, hymns, rules for worship and advice for ordinary behaviour. The essence of a scripture is its main message, the part you can carry home after the reading is over. Essence means the heart of the teaching, not every difficult word at once.

Grade 4 does not ask you to master whole libraries. It asks you to know which book belongs to which faith and to explain a few true lessons.

### The scriptures in this sub-strand
- **Ramayan** — a Sanatan scripture telling the life of Lord Rama. You will look at the early parts called Bal kaand and Ayodhya kaand.
- **Kalpasutra** and **Uttradhyana** — Jain scriptures. The Kalpasutra tells the lives of the Tirthankaras and is recited in many communities during Paryushan. The Uttradhyana gives teachings and stories about right conduct.
- **Dhammapada** and **Sigalovaada Sutta** — Buddhist scriptures. The Dhammapada is a collection of the Buddha's verses. The Sigalovaada Sutta is the Buddha's advice to a young householder named Sigala.
- **Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji** — the eternal Guru and scripture of the Sikhs.

### Why the message is important
Without these teachings it is easy to think only of yourself. The scriptures you will meet speak about duty to parents, truthfulness, not hurting living beings, equality, and remembering God. A learner who listens can grow spiritually: prayer becomes more thoughtful, and friends are treated more fairly.

Appreciate a scripture by handling any copy you are shown with clean hands and a quiet voice. Do not put a sacred book on the floor, and do not pretend you have read a chapter you have not read.

keyWords.meaning: a sacred writing of a faith
the main message or heart of a teaching

examples.problem: A learner says the Dhammapada is a Sikh scripture and Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is a Jain text. How do you correct the match?
steps: The Dhammapada belongs to Buddhist teaching.
Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is the Sikh scripture.
Jain texts in this sub-strand are the Kalpasutra and the Uttradhyana.
examples.answer: Dhammapada is Buddhist. Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is Sikh. Kalpasutra and Uttradhyana are Jain.

activity.title: Sort the scriptures by faith
materials: Cards with the names of the scriptures
steps: Place headings for Sanatan, Jain, Buddhist and Sikh.
Put each scripture card under the correct faith: Ramayan; Kalpasutra and Uttradhyana; Dhammapada and Sigalovaada Sutta; Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
With a partner, say in one sentence why a message from scripture can matter in daily life.
If a classmate cannot see the cards clearly, read them aloud and let that learner place a card too.

summary: A scripture is a sacred writing, and its essence is its main message.
This sub-strand studies Ramayan, Kalpasutra, Uttradhyana, Dhammapada, Sigalovaada Sutta and Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.
Each book is kept with its own faith.

practice.question: What is a scripture?
practice.answer: A sacred book or collection of teachings of a faith.

practice.question: Which scripture in this sub-strand tells the life of Lord Rama?
practice.answer: The Ramayan.

practice.question: Name the Sikh scripture studied here.
practice.answer: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

lessons.title: Bal kaand of the Ramayan
objectives: Retell the main events of the Bal kaand at Grade 4 level.
State two lessons from Rama's early life.
lessons.intro: The Ramayan, traditionally linked with the sage Valmiki, is the story of Lord Rama. Bal kaand means the section of his childhood and youth. It is one of the early chapters this sub-strand asks you to know.
lessons.notes:
### Ayodhya and the princes
King Dasharatha ruled in Ayodhya. He had three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. After a sacred rite for children, four sons were born. Rama was the son of Kausalya, Bharata the son of Kaikeyi, and Lakshmana and Shatrughna the sons of Sumitra. The brothers loved one another. Lakshmana especially stayed close to Rama.

### With the sage Vishwamitra
While the princes were still young, the sage Vishwamitra asked the king for help. Demons were disturbing the sages' sacrifices. Dasharatha sent Rama and Lakshmana with the sage. The boys obeyed both father and teacher. They protected the sages' rites. Obedience here was not weakness. It was courage used in the service of a good request.

### The bow and the marriage
The princes travelled on to Mithila, where King Janaka had set a challenge: a great bow of Lord Shiva would be drawn by the prince fit to marry his daughter Sita. Rama lifted and broke the bow. He and Sita were married. The brothers were married in that season as well. Bal kaand closes this early life with duty, learning and a marriage founded on a worthy task, not on boasting.

### Lessons
- Obey parents and teachers when they send you to do what is right.
- Use strength to protect people who are doing good, not to frighten the weak.
- Brothers and sisters can be loyal instead of jealous.
- A great person can still be humble. Rama does not parade his victory.

These lessons are the essence to carry into class. You are not asked to recite the whole kaand.

keyWords.meaning: the Sanatan scripture that tells the life of Lord Rama
the early section of the Ramayan about Rama's childhood and youth
the city of King Dasharatha and Lord Rama

examples.problem: Why did Rama and Lakshmana travel with Vishwamitra, and what lesson does that give a learner who is asked to help a teacher?
steps: The sage needed protection so that worship would not be disturbed.
The princes went because their father asked them and the cause was right.
A learner can obey a fair request and use their energy to help, not to show off.
examples.answer: They went to protect the sages' sacrifices. Learners likewise help when a rightful elder asks them to do good.

activity.title: Read the lessons of Bal kaand
materials: A short retelling chosen by the teacher
steps: Listen to a brief retelling of Bal kaand from your teacher or an audio device.
In pairs, list the people: Dasharatha, the three queens, Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana, Shatrughna, Vishwamitra, Janaka and Sita.
Write two lessons from this early part of the Ramayan.
Discuss with another pair whether jealousy between brothers would have spoiled the story.

summary: Bal kaand tells of Rama's birth, his journey with Vishwamitra and his marriage to Sita.
Rama obeys his father and teacher and uses strength to protect the sages.
Loyalty in a family and humility are part of the message.

practice.question: Who were the parents of Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna?
practice.answer: King Dasharatha was their father. Kausalya was Rama's mother, Kaikeyi was Bharata's mother, and Sumitra was the mother of Lakshmana and Shatrughna.

practice.question: What test did Rama complete in Mithila?
practice.answer: He lifted and broke the great bow and so was able to marry Sita, daughter of King Janaka.

practice.question: Give one lesson from Bal kaand.
practice.answer: Obey parents and teachers when the task is right, or use strength to protect others, or stay loyal in the family.

lessons.title: Ayodhya kaand: a promise kept
objectives: Explain the exile of Rama and Bharata's response.
Apply the lesson of keeping a promise and refusing unfair power.
lessons.intro: A promise can cost someone their comfort. In Ayodhya kaand, Rama leaves home for fourteen years because his father's word must stand. His brother Bharata refuses to enjoy a throne that is not rightly his.
lessons.notes:
### The two boons
King Dasharatha wished to appoint Rama as the heir. Queen Kaikeyi had once been promised two boons. Manthara, a servant who was afraid of losing importance, stirred Kaikeyi's fear. Kaikeyi asked that Bharata be made heir and that Rama be sent to the forest for fourteen years. The king was heartbroken, but a king's word had been given.

Rama did not rebel. He accepted the exile so that his father would not be made a liar. Sita chose to go with him, and so did Lakshmana. They gave up the palace without hatred as their motive. The forest was a place of hardship, not a holiday.

### Bharata's refusal
Bharata was away when this happened. He returned to find his father dead from grief and the throne waiting. He did not say, 'Good, now I rule.' He went to the forest and begged Rama to come back. Rama would not break the fourteen years. Bharata placed Rama's sandals on the throne and ruled from Nandigrama as a caretaker, not as a greedy king. He would keep the kingdom in trust until Rama returned.

### Lessons for righteous living
- Keep a rightful promise even when it is uncomfortable.
- Do not grab a prize, a seat or a post that belongs to someone else.
- Brothers can refuse jealousy. Bharata's love is as important as Rama's obedience.
- Advice from a friend should be tested. Manthara's advice harmed a whole family.

At school, keeping a promise may mean doing the duty you accepted on the class rota. Refusing unfair power may mean giving back a prefect's badge you were handed by mistake, or not taking the best part in a play by pushing a friend aside.

keyWords.meaning: the section of the Ramayan in which Rama goes into exile
being sent away from home for a set time
a promise to grant a request

examples.problem: The teacher promises the class monitor's role to Neelam, then a friend tells Tom to grab the badge while Neelam is absent. What would Bharata's example suggest?
steps: Bharata would not take a place that belonged to his brother.
Tom should leave the role for Neelam.
If there is confusion, they ask the teacher instead of scheming.
examples.answer: Tom should not take Neelam's role. He should wait and let the teacher's word stand.

activity.title: Discuss the essence of Ayodhya kaand
steps: Listen to the account of Kaikeyi's two boons, Rama's exile and Bharata's visit to the forest.
In groups, discuss which action shows righteousness: grabbing the throne, or keeping it in trust.
Each group writes two lessons and reads them to the class.
Peer-teach a classmate who missed the story so they can retell Bharata's choice.

summary: Rama accepted fourteen years in the forest so his father's word would stand.
Bharata refused to treat the throne as his prize and ruled in Rama's name.
The essence is promise-keeping, loyalty and not grabbing power.

practice.question: Why did Rama go to the forest?
practice.answer: To fulfil his father's promise to Kaikeyi that Rama would live in exile for fourteen years.

practice.question: What did Bharata do with the throne?
practice.answer: He placed Rama's sandals on it and looked after the kingdom until Rama's return.

practice.question: Name one way to apply this kaand at school.
practice.answer: Keep a fair promise, or do not take a role, prize or seat that belongs to someone else.

lessons.title: Kalpasutra and Uttradhyana
objectives: State what the Kalpasutra and the Uttradhyana are.
Explain Jain lessons of ahimsa, truth and self-control from these scriptures.
lessons.intro: Jain families listen to scripture especially during holy seasons. Two texts named for this grade are the Kalpasutra and the Uttradhyana. Their essence is a careful life that does not harm and does not lie.
lessons.notes:
### The Kalpasutra
The Kalpasutra is a Jain scripture recited in many Shvetambara communities during Paryushan. It contains the life stories of the Tirthankaras, above all Lord Mahavira, and rules for monks and nuns. From Mahavira's life, learners can take a simple essence: he was born a prince, left comfort, and taught that every living being has a soul. Hurting that being for fun, for show or from anger is wrong. The scripture is listened to with clean clothes and a quiet mind in communities that observe this reading. We do not invent extra miracles to make the story louder.

### The Uttradhyana
Uttradhyana, the Uttaradhyayana Sutra, is another Jain scripture of teaching. It is valued for lessons on right conduct: telling the truth, keeping promises, bearing hardship without cruelty, and loosening the grip of greed. Stories in it are used to train monks and also to teach lay people. The essence for a child is practical. Do not take a classmate's rubber. Do not swear that a lie is the truth. Do not mock a person who chooses a simple lunch because their family is observing a fast.

### Applying the essence
- Walk carefully where insects gather, when you can do so safely.
- Tell a teacher the truth about a mistake before someone else is blamed.
- Share instead of hoarding every sweet.
- Use respectful names for Jain scriptures and for the Tirthankaras.

If you visit a derasar or a community library, ask before you touch a sacred book. Some copies are kept for trained readers. Appreciation can be as simple as sitting still while a story is read.

keyWords.meaning: a Jain scripture of the lives of the Tirthankaras, recited in many communities at Paryushan
a Jain scripture of teachings about right conduct
the twenty-fourth Tirthankara, whose life is told in the Kalpasutra

examples.problem: A learner finds a lost sharpener and puts it in their pocket because nobody saw. Which teaching of these Jain scriptures speaks to that moment?
steps: Taking what is not given breaks the spirit of asteya taught alongside these texts.
Truthfulness would mean handing the sharpener to the teacher.
Ahimsa also includes not harming the owner by selfishness.
examples.answer: Hand the sharpener to the teacher. Do not keep what is not yours.

activity.title: Lessons from the Jain scriptures
materials: A short reading supplied by the teacher
steps: Listen to a short account of Mahavira from the Kalpasutra tradition and one teaching idea from the Uttradhyana, told by your teacher or an audio device.
Write the essence in your own words: respect for every living being, truth, and not taking what is not given.
Discuss with peers where a Grade 4 learner can apply each point this week.
If the class visits a library or community centre, list one rule for handling books with respect.

summary: The Kalpasutra tells the lives of the Tirthankaras, especially Mahavira.
The Uttradhyana teaches right conduct.
Their essence for learners is ahimsa, truth and honesty with other people's things.

practice.question: When do many Jain communities listen to the Kalpasutra?
practice.answer: During Paryushan.

practice.question: What is one lesson from Mahavira's life as told in that tradition?
practice.answer: Every living being has a soul and should not be harmed.

practice.question: What kind of teaching does the Uttradhyana give?
practice.answer: Teaching about right conduct, such as truthfulness, self-control and not being greedy.

lessons.title: Dhammapada and the Sigalovaada Sutta
objectives: Explain one lesson from the Dhammapada about hatred and love.
Name the duties the Sigalovaada Sutta gives to children, friends and families.
lessons.intro: Buddhist scripture is not only for monks. The Dhammapada speaks to anyone who feels angry. The Sigalovaada Sutta speaks to a young person about how to treat parents, teachers and friends.
lessons.notes:
### A verse on hatred
The Dhammapada is a book of short verses of the Buddha. One famous teaching says that hatred never ends by hatred. Hatred ends by love. This is an old law, not a new slogan. If someone insults you and you insult them back, the quarrel grows. If you refuse the insult and answer calmly, or ask a teacher for help, the chain can stop.

The same book teaches that the mind leads our actions. A kind thought makes a kinder word. A cruel plan makes a cruel act. Watching the mind is part of the essence: pause before you repeat gossip.

### Advice to Sigala
The Sigalovaada Sutta is the Buddha's counsel to Sigala, a young householder. It pictures duties in several directions, like points of care around a person:
- Towards parents: respect them, help them, and keep the family name honest. Parents in turn should care for their children.
- Towards teachers: listen, work hard and speak politely. Teachers should teach clearly and protect their learners.
- Towards friends: be generous, speak well of them, help them in trouble and keep promises. A false friend flatters you and disappears when you need help.
- Towards people who work in the home or the family business: treat them fairly, not harshly.

### Apply it this week
Greet parents politely and do one chore without being nagged. Thank a teacher. Keep a promise to a friend, such as returning a book on the day you named. If you are angry, wait and breathe before you speak. That is the Dhammapada's lesson in a school corridor.

Appreciate these scriptures by not twisting a verse into an excuse to stay silent when someone is being bullied. Love can include telling a trusted adult.

keyWords.meaning: a Buddhist scripture of the Buddha's verses
the Buddha's advice to the young householder Sigala on duties to other people

examples.problem: Two friends shout insults because each says the other started it. Which Dhammapada lesson helps, and what should they do?
steps: Hatred does not end hatred.
They stop the insults.
They can apologise or ask a mediator, such as a class teacher, to help them make peace.
examples.answer: They stop repaying insult with insult and seek a calm end to the quarrel.

activity.title: Duties around us
steps: Draw a learner in the middle of a sheet. Mark directions for parents, teachers and friends.
On each direction write one duty from the Sigalovaada Sutta in your own words.
Add the Dhammapada line in simple English: hatred does not end by hatred.
Discuss one real school quarrel and how love, or at least fairness, could end it. Include a classmate who wants help with writing by letting them dictate a sentence.

summary: The Dhammapada teaches that hatred ends by love, not by more hatred.
The Sigalovaada Sutta teaches duties to parents, teachers, friends and workers.
Learners apply this by polite help at home and by stopping insult contests.

practice.question: What does the Dhammapada teach about ending hatred?
practice.answer: Hatred is not ended by hatred. It is ended by love.

practice.question: Name two groups of people the Sigalovaada Sutta says we have duties towards.
practice.answer: Any two: parents, teachers, friends, or people who work for the family.

practice.question: Give one duty of a good friend according to this teaching.
practice.answer: Help them in trouble, speak kindly of them, be generous or keep promises.

lessons.title: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji
objectives: Explain what Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is and how it is honoured.
State the lessons of one God, equality, honest work and sharing.
lessons.intro: In a gurdwara the most honoured presence is not a wealthy guest. It is Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the scripture Sikhs revere as their living Guru. Understanding its essence helps the whole class respect a neighbour's place of worship.
lessons.notes:
### How the scripture came to be
Sikh tradition teaches that Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled the holy hymns into the Adi Granth. Later, Guru Gobind Singh Ji, the tenth Guru, added the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji and declared that after him Sikhs would take guidance from the Guru Granth Sahib, not from a human Guru. That is why the book is called Guru.

The hymns are in Gurmukhi script. They include the words of the Sikh Gurus and also of holy people from other backgrounds, such as Bhagat Kabir, Bhagat Farid, Bhagat Namdev and Bhagat Ravidas. Their presence in the scripture is itself a lesson: truth is not locked inside one caste or one community.

### The opening teaching
The scripture opens with the Mool Mantar. In simple English it proclaims one God, whose name is Truth, the Creator, without fear and without hatred, timeless, not born as creatures are born, self-existent, and known by the Guru's grace. You are not expected to recite the whole Guru Granth Sahib. You should understand that first message: God is one, and God does not hate.

### Three everyday rules
From the Guru's teaching, Sikhs often sum up a way of life a child can remember:
- **Naam japo** — remember God
- **Kirat karo** — earn by honest work
- **Vand chhako** — share what you have with others

Langar, the free kitchen, shows sharing. Anyone may sit and eat. Caste does not decide the row.

### Respect in the gurdwara
People cover their heads, remove shoes, bow, and do not turn their backs rudely on the scripture. The Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised seat under a canopy. A reader waves a whisk as a sign of honour. Appreciate this even if you are a visitor: follow the host's instructions and do not touch the scripture out of curiosity.

keyWords.meaning: the Sikh scripture honoured as the eternal Guru
the opening statement of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji about one God
earn your living by honest work

examples.problem: A visitor at a gurdwara keeps their shoes on and reaches out to flip pages of the Guru Granth Sahib to 'see the pictures'. What is the respectful action?
steps: Shoes are removed and the head is covered, as the hosts direct.
The scripture is not handled like a picture magazine.
The visitor sits, listens, and asks questions later in a quiet way.
examples.answer: Remove shoes, cover the head, and do not handle the scripture. Follow the gurdwara's guidance.

activity.title: The essence of the Guru Granth Sahib
materials: A device only if the teacher plays a respectful recording of kirtan
steps: Listen to your teacher explain how Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji became the Guru of the Sikhs.
Write the three phrases Naam japo, Kirat karo and Vand chhako with their meanings.
Discuss one way each phrase could appear in your school week.
If you use a search or a video, use only what the teacher approves, and write one new true fact in your own words.

summary: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji is the eternal scripture-Guru of the Sikhs.
Its opening teaching is one God, without fear and without hatred.
Remember God, work honestly and share with others.

practice.question: Who compiled the Adi Granth, and who declared the Granth to be the Guru after him?
practice.answer: Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled it. Guru Gobind Singh Ji declared it the Guru after the tenth Guru.

practice.question: What does the Mool Mantar say about God, in simple words?
practice.answer: There is one God, whose name is Truth, the Creator, without fear and without hatred.

practice.question: What do Kirat karo and Vand chhako mean?
practice.answer: Earn by honest work, and share what you have.

lessons.title: One message heard in four scriptures
objectives: Compare the lessons of the four faiths' scriptures without mixing up the books.
Choose one teaching from each to practise.
lessons.intro: The books are different, and their languages are different. Yet a Grade 4 class can hear a family likeness: tell the truth, do your duty, do not harm, and remember God. Comparing them fairly is a skill.
lessons.notes:
### A fair comparison
A fair comparison does not say that all scriptures are the same book. The Ramayan is not the Guru Granth Sahib. The Kalpasutra is not the Dhammapada. Each community has its own names, stories and ways of showing respect. A fair comparison asks: what does each one ask a child to do?

### Side by side
- **Ramayan:** obey a rightful promise, stay loyal in the family, and do not steal another person's place.
- **Kalpasutra and Uttradhyana:** do not harm living beings, do not lie, and do not take what is not given.
- **Dhammapada and Sigalovaada Sutta:** do not feed hatred, and carry out duties to parents, teachers and friends.
- **Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji:** remember one God, earn honestly and share.

If you swap the stories, you have not learned the essence. Bharata's sandals belong to the Ramayan. Langar belongs to the Sikh way. Ahimsa towards tiny living beings is taught with special care in the Jain texts. The verse on hatred is Buddhist.

### Apply without showing off
Choose one action from each column this month:
- Keep a rota duty you promised.
- Return a found item.
- Stop an insult before it grows.
- Share food or a pencil with someone who has none.

That is righteous living. It is more convincing than a poster that only copies long words.

### Speaking and listening
When you discuss, take turns. Listening is part of respect for scripture, because you cannot learn a message you keep talking over. Ask questions if a name is new. Correct a friend gently if they place a story in the wrong faith.

keyWords.meaning: to look at two or more things and notice what is alike and what is different
doing what is right and fair

examples.problem: A chart puts 'hatred ends by love' under the Ramayan and 'Bharata's sandals' under the Dhammapada. What is the correct placement?
steps: The teaching on hatred is from the Dhammapada.
Bharata and the sandals are from Ayodhya kaand of the Ramayan.
Each essence stays with its own scripture.
examples.answer: Move the hatred teaching to the Dhammapada and the sandals to the Ramayan.

activity.title: Four columns of essence
steps: Draw four columns, one for each group of scriptures.
In each column write two true lessons you have learned. Check them with the teacher so that no story is in the wrong column.
Discuss in groups how a class can apply one lesson from each column.
Teach a partner who was absent by explaining one column slowly.

summary: The scriptures are different books with a family of moral lessons.
Promise-keeping, ahimsa, ending hatred and honest sharing can all be practised at school.
Names and stories must stay with the correct faith.

practice.question: Match 'share what you have' with the correct scripture tradition in this sub-strand.
practice.answer: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (Vand chhako).

practice.question: Which scripture teaches that hatred does not end by hatred?
practice.answer: The Dhammapada.

practice.question: Why is it wrong to say all these scriptures are one and the same book?
practice.answer: Each faith has its own scripture, stories and way of showing respect, even when some moral lessons are similar.

lessons.title: Letting the message shape us
objectives: Show appreciation for scriptures through respectful habits.
Plan how the class will keep using one teaching after the topic ends.
lessons.intro: A lesson can be forgotten by the next morning. Appreciation becomes real when a scripture changes a habit: the way you speak to a parent, the way you handle a found coin, or the way you sit when a holy reading begins.
lessons.notes:
### Respect that anyone can show
You do not need to belong to a faith in order to appreciate its scripture. Appreciation looks like this:
- Listen when a story is read. Do not joke about names you find unfamiliar.
- Wash your hands before handling a book an adult tells you is sacred.
- Never draw cartoons that insult a Guru, a Tirthankara, Lord Rama or the Buddha.
- Ask a parent or a resource person when you want to know more, and use a search only with a teacher so that you do not land on unkind or untrue pages.
- If your class visits a temple, derasar, gurdwara, community centre or library, follow the rules of that place.

### From hearing to doing
Choose one teaching and write it as a personal rule in a full sentence. Examples that stay faithful to the scriptures you studied:
- 'I will not take a seat or a role that the teacher gave to someone else.'
- 'I will not harm an animal for fun.'
- 'I will not answer an insult with a worse insult.'
- 'I will share and I will not pretend another person's work is mine.'

Put the sentence where you will see it. At the end of the week, tell a partner whether you kept it. If you failed, begin again without lying about it. Truthfulness is itself a scriptural lesson.

### Spiritual growth
Spiritual growth does not mean sounding older than you are. It means prayer, worship or quiet remembrance becoming linked with behaviour. A person who recites and then cheats has missed the essence. A person who is still learning the words but returns a lost pen has caught a real piece of it.

Thank the classmates who helped you understand. Teaching a friend, especially a friend who needs the story repeated, is a good use of what you were given.

keyWords.meaning: to value something and show that value in your behaviour
something you do so regularly that it becomes part of you

examples.problem: A learner can retell Ayodhya kaand perfectly but still hides a classmate's pencil case as a joke. Has the essence been applied?
steps: Memory of the story is only the first step.
Hiding someone's property plays with taking what is not theirs.
Application would mean returning the pencil case and apologising.
examples.answer: No. The story has been memorised, but the teaching has not been lived until the pencil case is returned.

activity.title: A rule I will keep
steps: Each learner writes one rule drawn from a scripture in this sub-strand and names the scripture.
Share the rules in a circle. Listen to each speaker without interrupting.
Agree on one class rule, such as returning found items the same day, and write it on a chart.
Help a learner with special needs to place their rule on the chart by writing as they speak.

summary: Appreciation of scripture is shown by respectful listening and by fair behaviour.
One clear personal rule is better than a pile of forgotten quotations.
Spiritual growth joins the message to daily actions.

practice.question: Give two ways to show respect for a scripture.
practice.answer: Any two: listen quietly, handle it with clean hands, do not put it on the floor, do not mock it, follow the rules of the place of worship.

practice.question: Why is reciting a story without changing behaviour not enough?
practice.answer: The essence of scripture is meant to be lived. Cheating or hurting others after a reading misses the message.

practice.question: Write one personal rule based on any scripture in this sub-strand, and name the scripture.
practice.answer: A true rule tied to the right book, for example: I will not repay hatred with hatred, from the Dhammapada.

quiz.question: Which scripture tells the early life of Lord Rama in Bal kaand and Ayodhya kaand?
quiz.explanation: The Ramayan is the Sanatan scripture of Lord Rama's life.

quiz.question: In Bal kaand, Rama and Lakshmana went with Vishwamitra in order to
quiz.explanation: They obeyed Dasharatha and the sage and protected the holy rites.

quiz.question: What did Bharata place on the throne while Rama was in exile?
options: A crown of flowers for himself
quiz.explanation: Bharata ruled in Rama's name and would not treat the kingdom as his prize.

quiz.question: A learner who refuses to take a classmate's monitor badge is applying which lesson?
options: A rule about fasting at Paryushan only
quiz.explanation: Ayodhya kaand teaches promise-keeping and not taking what is another's.

quiz.question: The Kalpasutra is
options: A Jain scripture of the lives of the Tirthankaras
A book of the Buddha's advice to Sigala
The early section of the Ramayan
quiz.explanation: Many Jain communities recite the Kalpasutra during Paryushan.

quiz.question: Which lesson comes from the Dhammapada?
options: Hatred never ends by hatred; it ends by love
Guru Gobind Singh Ji declared the Granth as Guru
quiz.explanation: That verse is a famous teaching of the Dhammapada.

quiz.question: The Sigalovaada Sutta advises young people about duties to
quiz.explanation: The Buddha taught Sigala the duties owed in family, school and friendship.

quiz.question: Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji teaches learners to
options: Remember God, work honestly and share
Hide the scripture under a bed
Take any seat of honour by force
quiz.explanation: Naam japo, kirat karo and vand chhako sum up this way of life.

quiz.question: How should a visitor behave near Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji?
quiz.answer: Remove shoes, cover the head as directed, sit respectfully, and do not handle the scripture out of curiosity.
quiz.explanation: Appreciation includes the manners of the gurdwara.

quiz.question: Which action shows that a scriptural lesson has been applied?
options: Retelling a story and then hiding a friend's pencil case
Returning a found item and refusing to repay an insult
Mixing up the names of the books on purpose
quiz.explanation: Application means the message changes behaviour.

sources: KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 3.0 Scriptures, Sub-strand 3.1 Essence of Scriptures
